claims.text: An ab initio effective Hamiltonian coupled with Monte Carlo simulations can explicitly represent point defects and oxygen impurity states in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit treatment of defects and oxygen will improve agreement with conductivity measurements in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The relevant material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, inherent point defects, and local lattice distortions.
Monte Carlo simulations can capture temperature-dependent interactions among the defects represented by the effective Hamiltonian.
Impurity scattering dominates the conductivity behavior of oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Electron–phonon scattering and thermally activated defect dynamics become significant from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr induces defect states and local lattice distortions.
The oxygen-induced states and distortions cause band tailing and create charge-carrier scattering centers.
Idealized defect-free analytical models omit impurity-induced scattering.
Adding defect and impurity parameters to the Hamiltonian reduces predicted low-temperature conductivity through enhanced scattering.
Adding defect and impurity parameters alters the apparent high-temperature activation energy.
At low temperature, the proposed model will predict conductivity approximately 20–30% below perfect-crystal analytical predictions.
The model will predict a changed high-temperature Arrhenius slope corresponding to a modified activation energy.
Predicted room-temperature conductivity will be within ±10% of the measured value.
Traditional analytical approaches assume defect-free crystals and consequently overestimate conductivity, particularly for HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The hypothesis is applicable specifically to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Predictions may not remain valid at substantially different oxygen levels or outside the stated temperature ranges.
Defect-interaction parameterization can introduce quantitative uncertainty into conductivity predictions.
Failure to observe a 20–30% low-temperature reduction relative to defect-free predictions is proposed as a falsifying result.
A room-temperature model error greater than 30% is proposed as a falsifying result.
